credentials: PhD, Physical Anthropology (University of Minnesota, 1971); Professor, Washington State University, 1968-1998
stance: Flesh-and-blood zoological hypothesis; explicitly, publicly rejected paranormal/UFO/channeling framings. Proposed Sasquatch as a surviving relict population of Gigantopithecus blacki, evolving bipedalism and crossing the Bering Land Bridge into North America. Treated the 1969 Bossburg 'Cripplefoot' track casts as too anatomically precise (dermal ridges, dynamic toe-spreading, weight distribution) for a hoaxer to fake. Analyzed the Patterson-Gimlin film's gait -- persistent knee bend, high foot clearance, forward lean -- as biomechanically necessary for a 500+ lb animal walking upright. Argued the rarity of found remains matched the general rarity of finding any large wild mammal's carcass (bears, cougars) in dense forest, and that only a type specimen (a body) could secure formal species recognition.
key_publications: Big Footprints: A Scientific Inquiry into the Reality of Sasquatch (1992); Bigfoot Sasquatch Evidence (1999); 'Anatomy and Dermatoglyphics of Three Sasquatch Footprints,' Cryptozoology 2 (1983): 53-81; 'A Reconstruction of the Skull of Gigantopithecus blacki...,' Cryptozoology 5 (1987): 24-39
archive_location: National Anthropological Archives, Smithsonian Institution (Collection NAA.2003-21) — 7.38 linear feet, 9 series including a dedicated 'Sasquatch, 1963-2001' series
archive_access: Finding aid (categorized summary) is public domain (CC0), downloadable as PDF/XML. Raw documents (correspondence, notes) require an in-person appointment or scan request — not bulk downloadable, personal papers under estate terms

credentials: PhD, Wildlife Biology (University of Wisconsin-Madison); BSc Biology (University of Guelph); wildlife biologist for UN FAO across Africa, Asia, and the Caribbean; curator, BFRO, until his death in 2018
stance: Flesh-and-blood zoological/ecological hypothesis; classified Sasquatch as an undocumented North American great ape (Hominidae), not myth, spirit, or human hybrid. Placed heavy weight on cross-witness consistency -- mid-tarsal break foot biomechanics, chest-beating, wood-knocking, forward-slouched posture, specific vocalizations -- details he argued untrained observers were unlikely to invent. Treated dermal ridges and weight-distribution patterns in remote-area tracks as evidence against widespread hoaxing. Argued North America's contiguous temperate forests hold sufficient biomass to support a low-density, highly mobile population. Attributed the absence of remains to the same rapid scavenging/decomposition/soil acidity that makes finding any large wilderness mammal's carcass rare. In his 2010 book, argued the core barrier to recognition was scientific 'taboo' and cultural bias, not a genuine lack of evidence.
key_publications: North America's Great Ape: The Sasquatch (1998); The Discovery of the Sasquatch: Reconciling Culture, History and Science in the Discovery Process (2010)
archive_location: No dedicated public archive identified. A full biography, 'Sasquatch Discovered: The Biography of Dr. John Bindernagel' by Terrance N. James (2022, Hancock House), likely draws on his personal papers as source material
archive_access: Not yet located as a standalone archive — the biography is the closest current access point to his working materials

credentials: Field investigator (no academic credential); major advocate for the Patterson-Gimlin film; acquired ownership rights over the film to protect and promote its research validity
stance: Flesh-and-blood hypothesis; explicitly rejected paranormal, extra-dimensional, or mystical theories, insisting the creature must be evaluated with standard zoological principles. Centered his life's work on the 1967 Patterson-Gimlin film -- managing its copyright and bringing it to biomechanics experts and Hollywood costume designers to argue a suit of that quality was implausible for 1967. Maintained that eyewitness testimony alone would never satisfy mainstream science, and that only a verifiable type specimen (body, bone, or tissue) would. Was famously outspoken within the research community against hoaxers, fabricated casts, and sloppy field work. Reflecting late in life on nearly 40 years of searching without proof, he told a friend: 'You know, I've spent over 40 years -- and I didn't find it. I guess that's got to say something.' (quoted in his National Post obituary by Christopher Murphy)
key_publications: Sasquatch/Bigfoot (1993, co-authored with Don Hunter; originally published as Sasquatch, 1973)

credentials: Journalist (University of British Columbia; MA Journalism, Columbia University); Royal Canadian Navy veteran; owner/editor, Agassiz-Harrison Advance; Mayor of Harrison Hot Springs; compiled a database of 3,000+ sighting/track reports
stance: Flesh-and-blood hypothesis; treated Sasquatch as an undocumented, physical primate rather than a ghost, alien, or supernatural entity. Applied investigative-journalism standards -- signed affidavits, corroborating timelines, physical print measurements -- to witness accounts rather than relying on folklore. Focused heavily on trackway evidence, arguing that deep, anatomically consistent 15-inch-plus footprints over long stretches reflected a real animal's weight and stride, nearly impossible to fake continuously. Consistently criticized mainstream academia for declining to seriously investigate the accumulated evidence. Kept a level-headed distance from disorganized expeditions and commercial gimmicks. Noted that never personally sighting a Sasquatch was double-edged: a source of lasting regret, but also, he believed, what preserved his credibility as an objective, impartial chronicler.
key_publications: Sasquatch: The Apes Among Us (1978); On the Track of the Sasquatch (1968); his own compiled incident database (public domain, already integrated into this app as john_green_incidents_clean.csv)
